theme: Praise the name of the LORD in his house
readingInstruction: Read Psalm 135. You read this psalm on Day 488 beside Daniel’s idols. Read it now as a hymn of the returned community, who sang it in the rebuilt temple, calling the servants of the LORD to praise.
settingTheScene: Psalm 135 is made largely of quotations from other parts of Scripture: Exodus, Deuteronomy, and the Psalms. It was a worship song for the second temple, calling the priests and Levites “who stand in the house of the LORD” to praise. It celebrates God’s greatness in creation and in history, and it ridicules idols. On Day 488 you read it beside the idols of Babylon. Today, notice how it pulls together the Chronicler’s themes: the temple, the Levites, God’s choice, and God’s mighty acts.
observation: “Praise the LORD! Praise the name of the LORD, give praise, O servants of the LORD, who stand in the house of the LORD” (vv. 1-2).
“For the LORD has chosen Jacob for himself, Israel as his own possession” (v. 4).
“For I know that the LORD is great, and that our Lord is above all gods” (v. 5).
“Whatever the LORD pleases, he does, in heaven and on earth” (v. 6).
“He it was who struck down the firstborn of Egypt” (v. 8).
“Your name, O LORD, endures forever, your renown, O LORD, throughout all ages” (v. 13).
“Those who make them become like them, so do all who trust in them” (v. 18).
“O house of Israel, bless the LORD! O house of Aaron, bless the LORD! O house of Levi, bless the LORD!” (vv. 19-20).
interpretation:
The psalm is a collage of Scripture, and that is its point. The worshipers of the second temple did not invent new words. They drew on the Torah and the earlier Psalms, weaving them into a new song. This is how worship grows: from the word of God into the heart of the people.

The first section calls the servants of the LORD to praise. The reason is that the LORD has chosen Jacob. The word “possession” is a treasure, a special possession. Israel is not great, but God chose them, and this is the ground of their joy.

The psalm then looks at God’s power in creation and at his deeds in Egypt. “Whatever the LORD pleases, he does.” He sends lightning with the rain, brings the wind from his storehouses, and strikes down the firstborn of Egypt. He gave Israel the land as a heritage. These are not abstractions but stories, and they are told in order to say: our God acts.

At the center is the contrast with the idols, as in Psalm 115. The language is almost the same, which tells us how deep it ran in the memory of the community. Idols are silver and gold. They have mouths, eyes, ears, but no breath. “Those who make them become like them.” The community that remembered Babylon’s idols had a vivid sense of how empty they were.

The psalm ends by calling the whole community by name: house of Israel, house of Aaron, house of Levi, and “you who fear the LORD.” Each group is told to bless the LORD. It ends where it began: “Blessed be the LORD from Zion, he who dwells in Jerusalem! Praise the LORD!” The point is that the people who worship the living God are alive to him.
connection: Exodus 19:5-6 says Israel is God’s treasured possession. 1 Peter 2:9 applies it to the church: “a people for his own possession.” Ephesians 1:4 says he chose us in him before the foundation of the world. Isaiah 44:9-20 mocks idols. Revelation 4:11 says all things were created by his will. Psalm 115:3-8 parallels verses 15 to 18. Colossians 3:16: let the word of Christ dwell in you richly, singing.
application:
Compose a short prayer of praise using only words from Scripture, as the psalmist did.

Thank God that he chose you, not because of anything in you, but out of love.

Notice what in your life might be shaping you into its image. Are you becoming like what you worship?
prayerPrompts: Praise God for choosing you as his own possession.
Thank him that he is above all gods.
Ask him to keep you from idols.
